Fiber optic connectors, splices, and couplers are an important part of any fiber optic system.
INTRODUCTIONM

A fiber optic cable must be joined to the optical light source and the detector using specially designed connectors. Sections of cable are spliced together using another type of connector. Couplers allow a single optical signal to be distributed along different paths.
Connectors, splices, and couplers increase the versatility of a fiber optic system.

LESSON MENU
FIBER OPTIC CONNECTIONS
Different types of connectors add versatility to a fiber optic system. However, some signal loss must be expected for each connection. Most of these losses fall into one of two categories.
DISCUSSION
The first category we will discuss is misalignment.

The three different types of misalignment are lateral displacement, end separation, and angular tilt. Any of these may occur if the waveguide is not properly inserted into the connector, if the wrong type of connector is used, or if the connector is damaged.

Lateral displacement occurs when the waveguides are not aligned along their central axis. Recall that light propagation by total internal reflection is dependant upon the angle of incidence. The angle of incidence may be critically altered as light attempts to pass through the joint. The result is signal loss.
TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION - This phenomenon results when the first medium has a higher refractive index than the second medium and the angle of incidence is steep.
DEFINITION

Lateral displacement may also cause the light to miss the waveguide entirely and strike the cladding instead. Again, signal loss is the result. Lateral displacement losses are usually the highest misalignment losses incurred.

End separation means that the ends of the waveguides are too far apart or the gap between the waveguide and the optical light source/detector is too large. The light path will be altered as the beam traverses the gap and signal loss is the result. End separation losses are typically less than lateral displacement losses.

Angular tilt combines some of the problems of both lateral displacement and end separation. The angle of incidence may be changed and/or the light beam may strike the cladding. However, losses due to angular tilt are often the lowest of all the misalignment losses.
Which type of misalignment usually has the highest losses?
Losses due to angular tilt are often the lowest of all the misalignment losses.

Now we will discuss connector losses due to waveguide geometry. These types of losses involve fluctuations within the structure of the waveguides or varying characteristics of the waveguides.
Losses due to waveguide geometry occur because the two waveguides are mismatched in some way. The light signal cannot pass easily from the first waveguide to the second and signal loss results.

Concentricity losses occur when the waveguide's core is shifted and is not centrally located. Ellipticity losses occur when the core is too elliptical rather than circular. In either case, the light path may be altered or broken while attempting to travel from waveguide to waveguide since the cores do not align properly.

If the cores of the two waveguides are different sizes than a core diameter mismatch results. The cores will not align properly causing a change in the light path. The light path may also miss the core of the second waveguide and strike the cladding instead.
A cladding diameter mismatch results if the cladding of the two waveguides are different sizes. Once again, the cores will not align properly and the light path will be interrupted.

Using two waveguides with different numerical apertures (NA) results in an NA mismatch. Signal loss may result if the first waveguide has a larger NA than the second, but there is usually not a problem if the first waveguide has a smaller NA than the second.
You are splicing two different fiber optic cables together and you notice that the core of one waveguide is visibly off center. Should you question the use of this cable?

Using a fiber optic cable whose core is visibly off center may result in a concentricity mismatch. The light path may be altered or broken while attempting to travel from waveguide to waveguide since the cores do not align properly.......

Using the proper technique for splicing waveguides is important in order to limit losses to acceptable levels. High levels of signal loss may result if the ends of the fibers are not prepared correctly since a cracked or rough surface will affect the light path.

The proper method for cutting a glass waveguide involves scoring the waveguide's surface and pulling. The waveguide will break at the scored area. This method is similar to cutting a glass pane where the glass surface is scored with a diamond tool and the glass is broken along the scored edge.

Plastic waveguides are considered to be low quality fibers. The methods for cutting plastic waveguides are simpler than those for cutting glass waveguides. Common methods include using wire cutters or a hot knife.

Polishing the end of a waveguide can help ensure a smooth mirrored finish if the proper procedure is followed. Polishing kits include the appropriate jigs, polishing materials, and instructions. Chipped edges, uneven surfaces, and scratches may result if the instructions are not followed carefully. These conditions will cause signal loss. .

The two waveguides may be fused together or joined mechanically. A laser, plasma torch, or electric arc may be used to weld fibers together permanently. This is a delicate process and careful consideration must be given to details such as the amount of force used to join the waveguides as well as the alignment.

Mechanical splices allow two waveguides to be joined quickly by using shrink tubes, sleeves, or connectors. Some mechanical techniques are as permanent as fusing techniques. The fibers must be aligned correctly to avoid signal loss.

Splices are a necessary part of a fiber optic system since trying to run a single piece of mile long cable through a small opening is very awkward. Each splice, however, does mean some signal loss so the number of splices should be kept to a minimum. Splice losses should be below 0.5 dB and most losses are around 0.2 dB.

A variety of connectors are available for fiber optic applications. Connectors may be made of metal or plastic. Different connectors are available for multimode and singlemode waveguides. Some units are threaded and others use a clip-like mechanism for attaching cables or joining other components. RAPHICS TEXT)Connector Requirements 1. Low loss 2. Good environmental stability 3. Easy installation 4. Consistency: There should be the same amount of loss between the same type of connection. 5. Repeatability: Should be able to mate and demate connector many times without changes in loss. 6. Low cost
An acceptable fiber optic connector must meet at least these six requirements regardless of the connector's type or style.
4. Consistency: There should be the same amount of loss between the same type of connection.
5. Repeatability: Should be able to mate and demate connector many times without changes in loss.

FIBER OPTIC CONNECTIONS
In the first part of this experiment you are going to learn how to connectorize a plastic optical fiber, and in the second part you will observe the losses caused by a mechanical splice.
EXPERIMENT
We will be using the grey fiber optic cable to demonstrate the connectorization process. Wire cutters/strippers are required to cut the waveguide and a crimping tool is used to attach the connectors.
We will test the fiber optic cable after completing the connectorizing process. The cable will then be cut in half and rejoined using a mechanical splice.
1. Cut a piece of grey fiber optic cable that is 90 cm (3 ft) in length.

2. Strip off approximately 7 mm of the outer jacket of a cable with 18 gauge wire strippers. DO NOT use wire cutters to strip the outer jacket of a cable. Do not use strippers other than 18 gauge. Using inappropriate equipment may severely damage the waveguide resulting in unnecessary signal loss.

DO NOT use wire cutters to strip the outer jacket of a cable. Do not use strippers other than 18 gauge. Using inappropriate equipment may severely damage the waveguide resulting in unnecessary signal loss.
3. Place the crimp ring and grey connector over one end of the cable. Push the connector over the fiber until about 3 mm protrudes at the end. Do this for the blue connector also.
4. Carefully position the ring so that it is entirely on the grey connector and crimp the ring into place. Do this for the blue connector also.

The reason that there are two separate colors for connectors is for identification purposes only. Both the blue and grey connectors are the same mechanically. The grey matches up with the transmitter and the blue matches up with the receiver.
5. Any excess fiber protruding from the connector end may be cut off, however, ensure that at least 1.5 mm of fiber extends from the connector.
6. Look at the bottom of your polishing fixture. If any of the four dots are not visible, replace your polishing fixture with a new one.
7. Insert the grey connector into the polishing fixture with the trimmed fiber protruding from the bottom of the fixture.

8. Place the 600 grit abrasive paper (dark grey) on a flat, smooth surface. Pressing down on the connector, polish the fiber and the connector using a figure eight pattern of strokes. Do this until the fiber is flush with the polishing fixture.
9. Wipe the fiber and the polishing fixture clean with the tissue.

10. Place the flush connector and polishing fixture on the dull side of the 3 mm pink lapping film and continue to polish the fiber and connector for approximately 25 strokes. Remove the connector from the fixture. The fiber should be flat, smooth, and clean.
11. Repeat steps 7 through 10 with the blue connector. with the trimmed fiber protruding from the bottom of the fixture.
